question: Can feature learning in a deep neural network remain nontrivial and initialization-independent at infinite width, be reduced to self-consistent time-dependent activation and backpropagation kernels, and be computed accurately beyond static-NTK, gradient-independence, and small-feature-learning approximations?

key_findings.claim: The paper constructs a deterministic infinite-width description in which layerwise feature kernels and gradient kernels jointly determine hidden-field distributions, the evolving neural tangent kernel, and prediction dynamics.
key_findings.evidence: Under N and γ tending to infinity with γ0=γ/sqrt(N) fixed, the paper defines two-time kernels Φ and G and response kernels A and B. A Martin-Siggia-Rose-De Dominicis-Janssen path integral yields saddle equations whose single-neuron fields are coupled Gaussian-process transforms, with the kernels recovered as self-consistent moments.

key_findings.claim: The infinite-width feature-learning process itself is not new: at γ0=1 the authors explicitly recover the stochastic process previously derived by Yang and Hu with Tensor Programs IV.
key_findings.evidence: The contribution list describes an alternative derivation, Appendix N maps the parameterization to maximal-update parametrization, and Appendix N.6 gives a variable-by-variable dictionary between the DMFT and Tensor Programs recursions before concluding that their stochastic processes are identical.

anchors.section: N.6 Equivalence of DMFT at γ0=1 and Tensor Programs

key_findings.claim: For deep linear networks, the stochastic self-consistency closes into algebraic matrix equations, while the small-γ0 analysis predicts that the first nonzero kernel correction is order γ0 squared and that relative NTK movement scales as γ0 squared times depth.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 11 expresses H and G through causal response matrices and matrix inverses. Sections 5.2 and P show that odd powers through cubic order vanish under Gaussian symmetry, derive the leading corrections, and sum layer contributions to obtain relative kernel movement of order γ0^2 L.

anchors.section: P.2.1 Leading Corrections to the Φ Kernel
P.6 Form of the Leading Corrections / Equation 167

key_findings.claim: The proposed nonlinear solver replaces the exact Tensor Programs computation with an alternating Monte Carlo fixed-point iteration whose per-iteration algebra is polynomial but expensive in sample count and time resolution.
key_findings.evidence: Algorithm 1 repeatedly samples correlated Gaussian fields, solves the implicit single-site equations, estimates feature, gradient, and response kernels, and damps updates. Table 1 assigns full DMFT O(P^2 T^2) kernel memory and O(P^3 T^3) time, so it is cheaper than simulating a width-N network only when N is much larger than PT.

key_findings.claim: The strongest direct nonlinear agreement test is accurate but very small: a depth-4 tanh MLP is trained on only ten CIFAR-10 points, and only the width-convergence alignment panels report repeated-run uncertainty.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 1 compares loss, preactivation densities, final kernels, and two-time kernel summaries for P=10, L=3, and N=2500. The width sweep reports cosine alignment approaching one around N≈500 with standard deviations over ten repeats. The checklist states that all other experiments use one wide-network run.

anchors.section: NeurIPS checklist / Error bars and experimental details

key_findings.claim: Deep-linear experiments support the exact algebraic DMFT and show that static NTK, leading perturbation, and gradient-independence approximations can fail as feature-learning strength or depth grows.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 2 compares N=1000 networks on P=20 examples across depths and shows increased kernel displacement with depth. Figure 4 uses an L=5, N=1000, P=100 linear network and shows that the non-perturbative DMFT tracks loss and kernels where the three approximations deviate.

key_findings.claim: The weight-decay extension predicts a nonzero feature-learning fixed point for homogeneous networks where the lazy infinite-width limit collapses to the zero predictor.
key_findings.evidence: The paper derives a final-NTK kernel regressor with effective regularization and reports an N=1000, one-hidden-layer ReLU example at λ=1 in which increasing γ0 lowers final loss and increases target alignment, while γ0 tending to zero yields K and f tending to zero.

anchors.section: J Networks Trained with Weight Decay

key_findings.claim: The realistic CNN experiment does not evaluate numerical DMFT predictions; it only checks an associated width-rescaling hypothesis on two widths, two CIFAR-10 classes, and minibatch training.
key_findings.evidence: Figures 5 and 10 contain finite CNN curves for N=250 and 500 but no theoretical DMFT curve. The task is boat-versus-plane classification, and Appendix C.2 specifies batch size 250 despite the main derivation using full-batch gradient flow. Thus the plots support approximate width consistency under the prescribed scaling, not quantitative correctness of the self-consistent kernels on realistic data.

anchors.section: 6 Feature Learning Dynamics is Preserved at Fixed γ0

key_findings.claim: The asymptotic result is explicitly limited to fixed data count and fixed training horizon before width tends to infinity, excluding proportional-data, late-time, and many-output regimes relevant to practice.
key_findings.evidence: Section 3 takes t and P to be O(1), the multi-output extension keeps output count O(1), and the discussion warns that regimes such as P/N=O(1) or T/log N=O(1) may behave differently. The Langevin appendix separately notes that taking width to infinity before long time need not match taking the equilibrium limit first.

anchors.section: K Langevin Dynamics / order of limits

key_findings.claim: The path-integral derivation establishes stationary equations heuristically, not a theorem selecting a unique stable physical saddle.
key_findings.evidence: The main derivation assumes exponential saddle dominance and local stationarity. The authors explicitly call the technique non-rigorous. No contour deformation, uniqueness argument, Hessian stability condition, or treatment of multiple fixed points is supplied for the nonlinear saddle or the alternating solver.

anchors.section: 3.2 Deriving the DMFT Equations from the Path Integral Saddle Point

key_findings.claim: The nonlinear Monte Carlo procedure is not specified well enough to reproduce its numerical error or establish convergence.
key_findings.evidence: Algorithm 1 takes a sample count S and stops when kernels are 'not converged,' but the paper reports neither the S values, a convergence norm or tolerance, covariance regularization, numerical grid, nor error versus S. It reports β=0.6 and roughly 15 iterations for depth 4, while Figure 6 acknowledges noisy density estimates from finite sampling.

key_findings.claim: Much of the kernel validation uses cosine alignment, which can be near one despite an incorrect kernel magnitude, and most finite-network comparisons do not quantify initialization uncertainty.
key_findings.evidence: Section 4 defines validation as normalized trace alignment. Figures 1, 4, and related plots emphasize that alignment, whereas only Figure 1's width sweep has ten-repeat error bars; the paper's checklist says the other plots are single wide-network runs because concentration is expected.

anchors.section: 4 Solving the Self-Consistent DMFT / alignment metric

key_findings.claim: The stated smooth-activation assumption is not reconciled with the paper's ReLU experiments and higher-order perturbation formulas.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 1 assumes a twice-differentiable activation, and Appendix P invokes derivatives through fourth order. Figures 3 and 6 and the CNN experiments use ReLU. ReLU derivatives are well defined almost everywhere for first-order backpropagation, but the paper does not state or prove a nonsmooth extension for the saddle response and perturbation arguments.

anchors.section: P.2 Nonlinear Perturbation Theory / derivatives through fourth order

key_findings.claim: The empirical optimizer does not exactly match the central gradient-flow theory, and the paper leaves even the continuous-time recovery of its discrete-time DMFT unfinished.
key_findings.evidence: The main prediction equation uses the continuous chain rule and full-batch gradient flow. Appendix C trains with fixed-step JAX gradient descent, with minibatches for CNNs. Appendix M says the NTK ceases to be the key player in discrete time and explicitly leaves verification that its discrete equations recover NTK-governed function evolution in the continuous-time limit to future work.

anchors.section: M Discrete Time / Equation 132 and open verification

key_findings.claim: The published CNN pseudocode executes one fewer hidden convolution than its L variable claims and leaves one initialized convolution tensor unused.
key_findings.evidence: Initialization creates the first convolution, L-1 more convolution tensors, and a readout, so len(params)-1 equals L. Evaluation applies the first convolution and then loops over range(1,L-1), using only parameter indices 1 through L-2 before reading params[-1]. Parameter index L-1 is never applied, so the active network has L-1 hidden convolutions rather than L.

key_findings.claim: The same CNN pseudocode reuses a JAX random key for the final initialized convolution tensor and the readout vector, contradicting its independent-Gaussian initialization description even though the duplicated convolution is also unused by the forward pass.
key_findings.evidence: Inside initialization, each loop iteration splits key and draws a convolution with the retained key. After the last iteration, the code draws the readout with that unchanged key. JAX key reuse deterministically couples the two arrays rather than creating independent samples; the off-by-one forward loop happens to prevent the duplicated convolution tensor from affecting outputs.

key_findings.claim: Two main comparison figures contain metric or parameter-label inconsistencies that make exact replication ambiguous.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 5 labels panel b and its caption as classification error, but the y-axis says Test Accuracy and the increasing curves behave as accuracy. Figure 4's caption describes a network at γ0=1.0 while panels b and c are labeled γ0=1.5. Neither discrepancy is resolved in the text.

key_findings.claim: The finite-width appendix sketches a Gaussian fluctuation theory but does not justify interpreting the dynamical response-field action as an ordinary positive Gibbs density.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix P.7 changes the action's sign, calls exp(-NS) a Gibbs measure, expands around a saddle, and identifies an inverse Hessian as a covariance. The underlying MSRJD construction uses imaginary conjugate fields, and the paper neither proves a real positive contour nor checks that the Hessian is positive and invertible; it also says the exhaustive Hessian terms were not actually computed.

anchors.section: P.7 Perturbation Theory in Width N / Equations 168-171

method.core_idea: Replace the evolving weights of a rich, infinite-width neural network by deterministic layerwise two-time kernels and response functions, derive their coupled laws as a dynamical path-integral saddle, and solve those laws algebraically for linear networks or by damped Monte Carlo fixed-point iteration for nonlinear networks.
method.mechanism: The network is placed in a mean-field scaling with γ0=γ/sqrt(N) fixed. Forward activations and backward gradients define empirical kernels Φ and G. Delta-functional constraints and Gaussian weight integration produce an MSRJD action over Φ, G, their conjugates, and feedforward-feedback response kernels A and B. At a stationary action, each neuron becomes an independent draw from Gaussian processes whose covariances are the neighboring-layer kernels plus causal, data-dependent response terms. Moment and Jacobian averages of those single-site processes close the kernels. The resulting time-diagonal NTK drives predictions in gradient flow. Deep-linear Gaussianity closes the equations exactly; nonlinear fields are sampled and iterated to self-consistency.
assumptions: All hidden widths tend jointly to infinity at fixed ratios while depth remains fixed.
The feature-learning scale γ0=γ/sqrt(N) remains O(1); γ0 tending to zero is the lazy NTK endpoint.
Training-sample count P and observed time horizon T remain O(1) as width grows.

The principal prediction dynamics use full-batch continuous-time gradient flow; the main MLP experiments approximate it with fixed-step full-batch gradient descent and CNN experiments add minibatch noise.
Weights begin as zero-mean unit-variance Gaussian variables, with the independence structure assumed by the path integral.
The activation is twice differentiable in the main setup, with additional derivatives required by the nonlinear perturbation expansion.
Kernel order parameters concentrate over initialization strongly enough to replace finite-network empirical kernels by deterministic limits.
The MSRJD functional integral is dominated by a relevant stationary saddle, and that saddle gives the physical stochastic process.
The nonlinear self-consistency map has a stable solution reached by damped alternating Monte Carlo from the chosen initial kernels.
Gaussian-process covariance matrices and the causal operators needed for sampling, Jacobians, and deep-linear inverses are numerically well conditioned.
The number of output channels remains O(1) in the stated multi-output extension.
Cosine alignment, selected loss curves, and sampled marginal densities adequately test the predicted kernels despite limited repeated-run uncertainty.
Width comparisons at N=250 and N=500 are already in a concentration regime representative of the infinite-width scaling.
Nonsmooth ReLU experiments inherit the smooth-activation theory through an unstated almost-everywhere or limiting argument.
For equilibrium extensions, taking width to infinity before long time is informative even though the reverse order may differ.

techniques.role: Encodes forward and backward training trajectories with functional delta constraints and averages over random initialization.
Compresses population-wide activations and pregradients into Φ and G indexed by samples and two training times.
Uses A and B Jacobian averages to retain forward-backward correlations discarded by gradient independence.
Turns the large-width path integral into coupled moment equations at a saddle point.
Represents every neuron as an independent draw from Gaussian fields transformed by causal feature-learning feedback.
Builds the evolving tangent kernel from layerwise products of feature and gradient kernels to drive gradient-flow predictions.
Eliminates Monte Carlo for linear activations by solving matrix covariance and response equations.
Samples Gaussian processes, solves implicit fields, estimates moments and Jacobians, and damps kernel updates to a numerical fixed point.
Varies γ0 continuously from static NTK behavior to maximal-update feature learning.
Expands kernels around γ0=0 and identifies the leading order γ0-squared correction and its depth dependence.
Sets A and B to zero to isolate the importance of forward-backward weight correlations.
Tests the predicted equivalence under N→RN and γ→γ/sqrt(R) using finite CNN widths.
Sketches O(N^-1/2) kernel fluctuations by expanding the action around the infinite-width saddle.
Maps the modified NTK scaling and stochastic fields to maximal-update parameterization and Tensor Programs notation.
Checks the supplied CNN initialization and forward loops against the claimed depth and independent Gaussian initialization.

evaluations.setting: Depth-4 tanh MLP with N=2500 trained by MSE on a P=10 CIFAR-10 subset, plus a width sweep at fixed γ0
evaluations.metric: Training loss, preactivation density, final and two-time Φ/G kernels, and cosine alignment to DMFT
evaluations.result: DMFT curves visually match the finite network; ten-repeat alignment approaches one around width 500, with layer-dependent finite-width error
evaluations.baseline: The same finite network at lazy γ0=0 and rich γ0=1, with empirical kernels across widths

evaluations.setting: Deep linear networks on P=20 points with N=1000 and depths L=2 through 5
evaluations.metric: Loss, final H kernels, temporal H/G summaries, and displacement from initialization
evaluations.result: Algebraic DMFT tracks network curves and predicts larger feature-kernel displacement at greater depth
evaluations.baseline: Finite-width networks at the same γ0 and their initial kernels

evaluations.setting: One-hidden-layer ReLU network with N=1000 and weight-decay coefficient λ=1
evaluations.metric: Training loss and final feature-kernel alignment to the target
evaluations.result: Larger γ0 gives a lower nonzero fixed-point loss and greater target alignment; γ0 tending to zero yields the trivial zero-kernel predictor
evaluations.baseline: Lazy infinite-width NTK behavior under the same weight decay

evaluations.setting: L=5 deep linear network with N=1000 and P=100 over a range of γ0
evaluations.metric: Loss, final kernels, temporal kernel summaries, and kernel cosine alignment
evaluations.result: Full non-perturbative DMFT stays close to the network at strong feature learning where static NTK, leading perturbation, and gradient-independence curves deviate
evaluations.baseline: Static NTK, order-γ0-squared perturbation theory, and A=B=0 gradient independence

evaluations.setting: One-hidden-layer ReLU network with N=2000 across γ0 values up to 3
evaluations.metric: Loss, final h/z marginal densities, and final Φ/G kernels
evaluations.result: DMFT follows loss and kernel structure and captures non-Gaussian heavy-tailed hidden fields qualitatively, while the authors note finite-sampling noise in density estimates
evaluations.baseline: The corresponding finite-width network and the small-γ0 near-Gaussian regime

evaluations.setting: L=3 tanh network with N=2000 on synthetic class-structured data
evaluations.metric: Loss, final Φ/G kernels, and two-time kernel traces
evaluations.result: DMFT visually reproduces the finite network's loss and class-block kernel structure
evaluations.baseline: The same network at γ0=0 and γ0=1

evaluations.setting: Depth-5 CNN on boat-versus-plane CIFAR classification with channels N=250 and 500
evaluations.metric: Test MSE, a curve whose axis is test accuracy but caption calls classification error, and last-layer target alignment
evaluations.result: Curves are broadly similar across the two widths at fixed γ0, and larger γ0 trains faster and changes the kernel more
evaluations.baseline: Cross-width comparison at fixed γ0; no numerical DMFT curve is computed

evaluations.setting: Claimed depth-7 CNN on two-class CIFAR with N=250 and 500 over γ0 from 1 to 30
evaluations.metric: Test MSE, test accuracy, and last-layer target alignment over up to roughly 20,000 updates
evaluations.result: Loss and prediction curves show approximate width consistency, deeper kernel alignment has visible finite-size deviations, and final test accuracy is roughly insensitive to γ0
evaluations.baseline: N=250 versus N=500 for each γ0; again no full DMFT prediction

evaluations.setting: Reported nonlinear solver behavior for a depth-4 network
evaluations.result: The authors report convergence in about 15 iterations with β=0.6, but omit sample count S, tolerance, grid, and repeated solver error
evaluations.baseline: No solver-accuracy or runtime scaling ablation is reported

limitations: Author-stated: the dynamical field theory is heuristic and not entirely rigorous.
Author-stated: the asymptotics hold for P and T of order one and may fail in proportional-data or late-time regimes.
Author-stated: full DMFT costs O(P^3 T^3) time and O(P^2 T^2) kernel memory and is advantageous over direct simulation only when N is much larger than PT.
Author-stated: the nonlinear density estimate can be noisy because the self-consistency moments are estimated with finitely many Monte Carlo samples.
Author-stated: fixed-width deviations become more important in deeper feature kernels, while the finite-width and equilibrium appendices leave major questions open.
Reviewer-identified: exact numerical DMFT validation is limited to tiny data sets, with P=10 for the flagship nonlinear CIFAR subset and P≤100 for the main controlled comparisons.
Reviewer-identified: the realistic CNN plots validate only a two-width scaling pattern, not the quantitative DMFT solution, and use only two CIFAR classes.
Reviewer-identified: the CNN optimizer uses batch size 250 and discrete steps, outside the main full-batch gradient-flow derivation.
Reviewer-identified: all finite-network experiments except Figure 1's width sweep are single runs, so initialization and minibatch uncertainty are not quantified.
Reviewer-identified: cosine kernel alignment is insensitive to scale error and therefore cannot by itself establish correct kernel magnitude or NTK eigenvalues.
Reviewer-identified: Algorithm 1 omits the Monte Carlo sample count, stopping rule, time grid, conditioning procedure, covariance jitter, and error-versus-compute study.
Reviewer-identified: no proof establishes existence, uniqueness, or convergence of the nonlinear fixed point, nor selection of the relevant saddle.
Reviewer-identified: the smooth-activation assumptions do not cover the ReLU experiments or the higher-order ReLU perturbation formulas as written.
Reviewer-identified: the discrete-time appendix does not verify recovery of the continuous-time NTK dynamics that motivate the main empirical comparison.
Reviewer-identified: the supplied CNN forward loop omits one initialized hidden convolution and therefore does not implement its claimed L-layer architecture.
Reviewer-identified: the CNN initializer reuses a JAX key for the final convolution tensor and readout and does not implement fully independent Gaussian draws.
Reviewer-identified: Figure 5 confuses accuracy with classification error, and Figure 4 inconsistently labels the compared γ0 value.
Reviewer-identified: the paper does not specify CIFAR split sizes, class balance, preprocessing, augmentation, total updates, optimizer implementation/version, seeds, or full result manifests.
Reviewer-identified: the finite-width inverse-Hessian construction treats a response-field action like a positive probability density without a contour or stability argument.
Reviewer-identified: output count and depth stay fixed, excluding joint width-depth, growing-class, and modern large-output asymptotics.
failure_modes: If P grows with N, sample-space kernel spectra and generalization can remain random or develop proportional-limit effects absent from fixed-P DMFT.
If training time grows with width, small finite-width errors can accumulate and the N→∞ then T→∞ limit can differ from training finite networks to convergence.
Multiple or unstable saddle solutions can cause the damped Monte Carlo iteration to depend on initialization, β, or sampling noise rather than select a unique physical process.
A nearly singular PT-by-PT covariance or causal operator can destabilize Gaussian sampling, Jacobian estimation, or the deep-linear inverse formulas.
Monte Carlo rank deficiency at small S can bias kernel estimates; damping can hide rather than remove that bias without an S and tolerance sweep.
Cosine alignment can report near-perfect agreement when the theory predicts the wrong eigenvalue scale, learning rate, or output dynamics.
ReLU kinks can invalidate response derivatives or higher-order expansions that assume smooth activations, especially for mass concentrating near zero.
Minibatch noise, finite step size, momentum, or adaptive optimizers can produce dynamics that are not captured by the central full-batch gradient-flow NTK equation.
At large γ0 or depth, feature updates and kernel variance can compound, making widths 250-500 insufficient for concentration even if early loss curves look similar.
The fixed-γ0 width rule can appear successful over a factor-of-two width sweep but fail at later time, harder data, or much larger depth because finite-width bias is systematic.
An off-by-one implementation can make a claimed depth comparison actually train a shallower model and leave a parameter with zero gradient.
JAX key reuse can introduce deterministic dependence between purportedly independent parameters; correcting the unused-layer defect without splitting the key would make that dependence active.
Treating an indefinite or complex action Hessian as a covariance can yield negative variances or an invalid finite-width Gaussian approximation.
At equilibrium, exchanging infinite-width and long-time limits can select different predictors or posterior-like states.
High feature-learning strength can accelerate training without improving final generalization, as the deeper CNN experiment already suggests.
reusable_insights: Track activation and backpropagation kernels jointly: forward features alone miss correlations created by reusing each weight matrix in both passes.
Use a scalar feature-learning strength that interpolates between lazy and rich limits so approximations can be stress-tested continuously rather than at isolated parameterizations.
Separate a limit's existence from its numerical computability and from its fidelity at practical width; all three require distinct evaluations.
Validate time-dependent kernels with scale-sensitive Frobenius and spectral errors in addition to cosine alignment, and propagate those errors to prediction trajectories.
For stochastic self-consistency solvers, report sample count, random seeds, covariance regularization, stopping norm, tolerance, residuals, multi-start agreement, and S-by-grid convergence.
Pair fixed-width rescaling plots with explicit infinite-limit predictions on a tractable subset and with later-time finite-width bias measurements on the realistic task.
Test the order of limits empirically by sweeping width, data count, and training horizon together rather than only widening at fixed P and T.
Use matched gradient-flow and discrete-SGD experiments to identify whether a theory's success comes from the limit itself or merely from parameterization transfer.
Audit executable architecture depth by asserting which parameter tensors receive gradients and by comparing the declared and executed layer counts.
In JAX, split a fresh PRNG key before every random draw and unit-test that no key is reused.
For nonsmooth activations, formulate the response theory with weak derivatives or a controlled smooth approximation and check the smoothing limit.
Treat path-integral saddles as hypotheses until contour, stability, and multiple-saddle issues are resolved or numerically diagnosed.
Compare early-time concentration with late-time bias and variance; agreement in loss can coexist with disagreement in internal kernels or individual predictions.
Use later finite-width DMFT corrections as uncertainty estimates around infinite-width predictions rather than presenting the limit as an exact finite-network curve.
open_questions: Can the DMFT saddle and its stochastic process be derived rigorously for deep nonlinear networks, including existence, uniqueness, and a valid integration contour?
What replaces the fixed-P,T kernel closure when P/N, T/log N, depth/width, or output count/width remains finite?
Does the alternating nonlinear solver converge to the same solution across initial kernels, random samples, damping values, and time discretizations?
Can structured covariance methods, low-rank time bases, online DMFT, or data-averaged closures reduce O(P^3 T^3) cost while retaining non-perturbative feature learning?
How accurately do full DMFT values predict modern CNN, ResNet, and transformer representations on complete datasets rather than only width-rescaling consistency?
How should minibatch stochasticity, momentum, Adam, weight decay, and finite learning rates be incorporated in one validated function-dynamics theory?
Can the discrete-time DMFT be shown to recover the continuous-time NTK-driven equation, and can it predict edge-of-stability behavior without a small-step limit?
What smoothness conditions are actually necessary, and can ReLU and other nonsmooth activations be covered without informal almost-everywhere reasoning?
When do the N→∞ then t→∞ and t→∞ then N→∞ limits agree for gradient flow, Langevin training, and regularized predictors?
Can inverse-action-Hessian finite-width corrections be made mathematically valid and numerically tractable for deep nonlinear networks?
Do stronger feature updates improve test error after controlling for training speed, architecture, and effective regularization?
Would correcting the CNN pseudocode's omitted layer and random-key reuse materially change the reported width-consistency curves?
Which kernel statistic best predicts downstream generalization: alignment, spectrum, centered kernel-target alignment, or the full coupled prediction covariance?

competitive_landscape.title: Feature Learning in Infinite-Width Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: closest prior and equivalent infinite-width process
competitive_landscape.difference: Yang and Hu classify parameterizations and derive the maximal-update feature-learning limit with Tensor Programs, including exact applications to Word2Vec and MAML. The reviewed paper explicitly recovers the same γ0=1 stochastic process; its additional value is a DMFT kernel-order-parameter formulation, lazy-to-rich γ0 interpolation, response-kernel interpretation, and a different numerical fixed-point procedure.

competitive_landscape.title: Efficient Computation of Deep Nonlinear Infinite-Width Neural Networks that Learn Features
competitive_landscape.difference: Yang, Santacroce, and Hu introduce the π-limit of projected gradient descent, prove almost-sure width convergence with Tensor Programs, and compute deep nonlinear limits on full CIFAR-10 and Omniglot. It changes the optimizer away from ordinary gradient descent but scales to realistic data; the reviewed DMFT preserves ordinary rich gradient-flow dynamics yet costs O(P^3 T^3) and validates its numerical solution only on small P.

competitive_landscape.title: Dynamics of Finite Width Kernel and Prediction Fluctuations in Mean Field Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Bordelon and Pehlevan extend the DMFT program to O(width^-1/2) fluctuations, coupled kernel and prediction variance, online learning, discrete-time edge-of-stability effects, and significant CNN bias/variance corrections. It directly addresses the reviewed paper's deterministic infinite-width and single-run limitations and shows that deep rich networks can accumulate substantial kernel variance.

competitive_landscape.title: Feature-Learning Networks Are Consistent Across Widths At Realistic Scales
competitive_landscape.difference: Vyas et al. test width consistency across more architectures and harder settings, including ImageNet and language modeling, and separate initialization variance from systematic narrow-width bias. They find strong early-time agreement but growing late-time deviations on hard tasks, substantially qualifying the reviewed paper's factor-of-two, two-class CIFAR width evidence.

competitive_landscape.title: Adaptive kernel predictors from feature-learning infinite limits of neural networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Lauditi, Bordelon, and Pehlevan derive data-dependent kernel predictors for rich Bayesian networks and for weight-decayed gradient flow using DMFT fixed-point equations, then compare test loss with lazy kernels on benchmarks. This develops the reviewed paper's representer and weight-decay appendix into explicit stationary adaptive predictors and generalization evaluations, but focuses less on the complete transient two-time dynamics.

competitive_landscape.title: Global Convergence and Rich Feature Learning in L-Layer Infinite-Width Neural Networks under μP Parametrization
competitive_landscape.difference: Chen, Yang, Zhao, and Gu use Tensor Programs to show, under activation conditions, that SGD in the μP limit learns linearly independent features and that every convergent point is globally optimal. It addresses optimization guarantees absent from the heuristic saddle analysis, while the reviewed paper supplies more explicit time-dependent kernel observables and a numerical solver for finite data trajectories.

competitive_landscape.title: Understanding Scaling Laws in Deep Neural Networks via Feature Learning Dynamics
competitive_landscape.difference: Yao, Wu, and Gao derive coupled Neural Feature Dynamics for ResNets in a joint infinite-width and infinite-depth limit, identify when gradient independence becomes valid again, diagnose feature-learning collapse in deeper residual blocks, and propose a depth-aware correction. This tackles depth scaling held fixed by the reviewed DMFT and shows that its finite-depth gradient-independence failure need not extrapolate unchanged to an infinite-depth residual regime.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim the first self-consistent dynamical field theory for feature learning in deep infinite-width networks, a scalar interpolation between lazy and rich limits, a polynomial-time numerical solver for nonlinear saddle equations, exact deep-linear closure, and accurate prediction beyond common approximations.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Pages 2-10 state and evaluate the path-integral, self-consistency, interpolation, solver, deep-linear equations, approximation comparisons, and CNN scaling claims; Appendices B, D, F, M, N, and P give the algorithm, derivations, extensions, equivalence, and perturbative analyses.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: After comparison, the defensible novelty is not discovery of the rich infinite-width stochastic process, which the paper proves identical to Tensor Programs IV, but its expression as coupled time-dependent feature, gradient, and response kernels; the γ0 bridge to the lazy limit; deep-linear algebraic closure; and a damped Monte Carlo self-consistency recipe. The π-limit already offered a more scalable but optimizer-altered alternative. Later work supplies finite-width uncertainty, realistic-width failure diagnostics, adaptive fixed-point kernels, convergence guarantees, and joint-depth scaling. The reviewed formulation is conceptually reusable and its controlled small-P matches are persuasive, but the heuristic saddle, underspecified solver, limited realistic evaluation, optimizer mismatch, and concrete CNN pseudocode defects prevent treating it as a validated general-purpose predictor for practical deep learning.

reviewer_notes: Primary pass read all 55 cached pages and checked every appendix. Figures 1-10, Table 1, Algorithm 1, the CNN pseudocode, discrete-time equations, Tensor Programs dictionary, and finite-width Hessian construction were visually inspected against the PDF. The current target record was checked as arXiv v3 on 2026-08-23. Seven genuine adjacent or competing works were checked on primary arXiv or official OpenReview records, including the exact Tensor Programs prior, a contemporaneous scalable alternative, and follow-ups through 2026. The contradiction audit covers mathematical scope, numerical specification, empirical protocol, metric labels, and line-level pseudocode behavior. No external notebook bundle was available in the indexed corpus, so the audit of executable details is limited to code printed in the paper; findings do not assert results from an unseen repository. Author claims are separated from reviewer inference. This is a primary full-text reading, not a second-review verification.
